title: Acoustics for Supportive and Healthy Buildings: Emerging Themes on Indoor Soundscape Research
research_focus: To establish an initial discussion over open questions in the emerging field of indoor soundscape research, exploring the link between acoustic design and practices in health and well-being (e.g., regenerative, salutogenic, biophilic design approaches), and to encompass the characterization, management, and design of indoor soundscapes to potential health-related outcomes for occupants.

sample_context.description: Four experts (Jack Harvie-Clark, Jian Kang, Lisa Lavia, Antonella Radicchi) were selected based on their specific and complementary areas of expertise, cognitive diversity, and roles as researchers or practitioners in urban soundscape, indoor soundscape, acoustic design, and public health and well-being.
sample_context.setting: The study gathered expert perspectives on indoor built environments, rather than directly studying occupants in a specific physical setting.

findings.consequent: Underestimation of acoustic quality importance; acoustic requirements subjugated to visual ones
findings.description: Building design is primarily visually driven, leading to acoustic quality being underestimated and not prioritized at the project outset stage, often resulting in acoustic requirements being subjugated to visual ones.
supporting_quotes: Design at the moment is so visually driven

findings.antecedent: Complexity of acoustic experience in the built environment
findings.consequent: Need for further scientific evidence on acoustic quality impact from a perceptual and multisensory approach
findings.description: To understand and value the impact of acoustic quality for policy makers and practitioners, more scientific evidence is needed, assessed from a perceptual perspective and through a multisensory approach, integrating disciplines related to acoustics, sociology, psychology, and physiology.
supporting_quotes: We are living in a kind of transition phase and this is where we need a lot more evidence across soundscape
There is a need to cover a much more accurate picture of the foundational importance of acoustics to the interaction of the acoustic sense with all of the other senses

findings.consequent: Acoustic environment assessed based on perception in context, sounds valued as design resources, promoting positive effects of sound
findings.description: Soundscape research shifts from a traditional noise control approach to valuing sounds as potential resources for shaping healthy and supportive acoustic environments, offering flexibility in design and promoting positive effects of sound.
supporting_quotes: not just to consider sound as noise, or waste, but also as a resource
Soundscape is also a framework because there are many potential routes to meet the minimum specification. That is good news for designers and practitioners because it provides a lot of flexibility

findings.consequent: Design meets people's preferences, addresses complexity of user-building and building-city interactions, avoids unintended consequences
findings.description: Engaging users and relevant stakeholders in the building design process is mandatory to ensure that acoustic design meets people's preferences, addresses the complexity of user-building and building-city interactions, and reduces the risk of mismatches.
supporting_quotes: This is the core of the soundscape approach. We are interested in how people perceive and experience the acoustic environment in context ... it's mandatory to involve people not only in the evaluation but also in the design of buildings

findings.consequent: Different expectations, exposure times, and tasks for occupants
findings.description: People tend to spend more time indoors, performing a variety of tasks, often without the ability to choose better places, leading to different expectations and needs compared to outdoor urban spaces.
supporting_quotes: In outdoor spaces people may not stay as long and there may be much more choices where to stay. In a hotel atrium or in a museum for example, you often don't have many spaces to choose. Also, in indoor spaces people may have longer exposure to sound, such as in open plan offices ... There are many differences and also people's tasks are different

findings.consequent: Characterized by reverberant sound fields, combination of indoor and outdoor generated sounds
findings.description: Indoor spaces are characterized by reverberant sound fields that can amplify sound disturbance, and are affected by a combination of outdoor-generated and indoor-generated sounds transmitted through various paths.
supporting_quotes: Indoor spaces have reverberation associated, so the sound disturbance between sources can be stronger than outdoors

findings.consequent: Increased audibility of internal sounds (e.g., neighbors), potential for external desired sounds to mask internal unwanted sounds
findings.description: High insulation can make internal noises more annoying; facades and ventilation systems can be reinterpreted as filters to transmit desired outdoor sounds to mask unwanted indoor sounds, balancing against privacy needs.
supporting_quotes: The risk of having high insulation to the outside is that you might hear your neighbours more; and the sounds of your neighbours can sometimes be much more annoying than the sounds from outside. So, it can be useful to have some external desired sound from outside to mask unwanted sound from your neighbours otherwise you may need higher indoor sound insulation

findings.antecedent: Headphone use for personal acoustic control
findings.consequent: Increased personal space, reduced disturbance, but potential disconnection from environment; may indicate failure of acoustic design
findings.description: Using headphones allows individuals to curate their own acoustic environment and increase personal space, but it raises questions about whether this indicates a failure of the acoustic environment or a valid management tool, potentially leading to disconnection.
supporting_quotes: Music is a popular masking sound. Ideally, people like to hear their own music rather than other sources of sound. Maybe it's more important to provide the opportunity for people to shape their own sound environment with the sound they prefer

I have started to use headphones and I am surprised by the extent to which I feel unconnected to the rest of the office when I do that. It increases my personal space, to not be disturbed and interrupted ... But is it [wearing headphones] a failure of the acoustic environment or is it a good way to manage it?

findings.consequent: Improved description of human perceptual response to acoustic environment in POE surveys
findings.description: Current post-occupancy evaluation (POE) surveys should integrate soundscape methodologies to better describe the human perceptual response to the acoustic environment, moving beyond pre-determined rating schemes to allow for more free expression of feelings.
supporting_quotes: A better application of questionnaires and surveys methods [is needed] to gain information from people about their environment ... the soundscape theory has information about the type of survey methods that can be used

When I answer the questionnaires about my sound environment, I always feel that the questions are not quite the way in which I think about it or I would describe it. Interviews would be the best way to collect soundscape data

findings.consequent: Collection of feedback on acoustic environment, reconnection of participants to sensorial experience
findings.description: Soundwalks are useful for collecting feedback from participants and encouraging them to actively listen and reconnect with their sensorial experience of the environment, though their applicability to indoor sedentary tasks may require adaptation.
supporting_quotes: Usually when I lead soundwalks I have discussions with the participants. So, you not only collect feedback from the single participant, but you can also get feedback or patterns emerging from the group discussion, from the exchange that participants among them after the soundwalk

If you lead soundwalks with people you somehow invite them to reconnect with their sensorial experience of the places, you invite them to retune to their environment and this is something we are not so used to [because] we always wear headphones, we tend to stay detached somehow from the environment

findings.consequent: Autonomous collection of soundscape feedback from building users, reduced researcher bias
findings.description: Mobile apps allow building users to provide feedback on the perceived acoustic environment autonomously and when convenient, potentially reducing bias associated with active listening during researcher-led evaluations.
supporting_quotes: Through the use of mobile apps people can collect data; can give their feedbacks on the quality of the indoor places independently from the researchers. People can work autonomously, they are not influenced by the researchers and mostly they can collect the data when they feel they need to share and they want to provide feedback

findings.consequent: Broader picture of acoustic assessment, better explanation of human perceptual response
findings.description: Integrating psychoacoustic data with traditional methods and using binaural recordings improves the characterization of the physical acoustic environment and provides a better explanation of the human perceptual response in context.
supporting_quotes: Collecting psychoacoustic data helps to really broaden out the picture of the acoustic assessment of the environment and helps to explain the human perceptual response in context. So, better use of psychoacoustic data integrated with traditional methods is one very important thing
Better instrumentation [is needed] to measure and to collect better acoustic data based on psychoacoustics

findings.antecedent: Virtual reality technologies with accurate auralization
findings.consequent: Pre-construction soundscape assessments, potential building users experience future acoustic environments
findings.description: Virtual reality technologies, combined with accurate auralization, can help address the challenge of assessing soundscapes in non-existent buildings by enabling potential users to experience future acoustic environments in advance, supporting decision-making.
supporting_quotes: Auralization and visualization techniques can be used to support decision making and planning and help people to better assess the human perceptual response in context before things are completed

findings.antecedent: Natural sounds brought indoors (facade openings, materials, active systems)
findings.consequent: Enhanced connection to nature, masking of unwanted sounds
findings.description: Natural sounds can be introduced into indoor environments via facade ventilation openings, natural materials (e.g., wood, gravel), or active systems to enhance connection with nature and mask unwanted sounds.
supporting_quotes: You could somehow enhance the sonic stimuli coming from nature indoors if you work with different materials for pavements. You can use wood or gravel

findings.consequent: Perceived as 'fake', skepticism about effectiveness
findings.description: Some experts express skepticism about the effectiveness and authenticity of playing artificial natural sounds indoors, perceiving them as 'fake' and not a substitute for good acoustic design.
supporting_quotes: Personally, I don't like being played fake birdsong rather than real birds. I find recorded birdsong a bit fake
I am skeptical that you can get some good sonic stimuli from nature indoors unless you use augmented technology to do that. But I am not so much a fan of artificial soundscapes

findings.antecedent: Coherent combination of visual and audio stimuli related to natural elements
findings.consequent: Enhanced appreciation of the environment, mutual enhancement of components
findings.description: Visual and audio natural stimuli should be coherently combined to enhance each other and improve people's appreciation of the environment, supporting potential benefits like physiological stress recovery.
supporting_quotes: Sometimes, if we cannot connect to nature outside 100% visually, but we use sound, we can enhance it. Then the overall effect can be greater. And, vice versa. If you want people to appreciate outdoor sounds like water ... if people can't see it, then it can sound like white noise and people may be not happy A window would be good, otherwise you can have pictures of natural scenes

findings.consequent: Space suitable for a multitude of uses, not reliant on added sounds
findings.description: Good acoustics should be a foundational element of building design, making spaces fit for purpose for a multitude of uses, rather than strictly relying on added sounds which may change in preference over time.
supporting_quotes: Nothing replaces having good acoustics. Having good acoustics in the design of a building is the foundational element ... Like a concert hall that is designed to be able to play a range of types of music, if you have really good acoustics principles in the design of the building then you can put many kinds of music in there, it is fit for purpose for a multitude of uses

findings.consequent: Noise limits primarily based on annoyance, not other physical/mental diseases
findings.description: Current WHO guidelines for environmental noise are primarily set based on annoyance levels, suggesting a need to review them from a holistic perspective that includes non-acoustical factors and soundscape methods.
supporting_quotes: The limiting factor in every case for the environmental noise limits [in WHO Environmental Noise Guidelines for the European Region guidelines] was annoyance. So, the [WHO] guideline levels, which are external noise levels, are based on annoyance rather than other health impacts of noise

findings.antecedent: Sound level below a certain threshold
findings.consequent: Type of sound (positive/negative) becomes more important than decibel level for health outcomes
findings.description: Below a certain sound level threshold, the qualitative character of sounds (wanted vs. unwanted, positive vs. negative) is more critical for health and well-being than the absolute decibel level, although very loud positive sounds can still be detrimental.
supporting_quotes: I think the principle is, below a certain level the type of sound is more important, if it's positive or negative. But above a certain level you need to be careful. Although sometimes with positive sounds people are happy, but it is not good for their health. For example, in a very loud disco people are happy, they are not annoyed, but that is not necessarily good for their ears and heart

findings.consequent: Acoustic boredom, as frustrating as a chaotic environment, both unwanted
findings.description: People desire calm but not monotonous environments; acoustic boredom is as unwanted and frustrating as a chaotic environment, indicating that perceptual response in context, not just decibel level, is key.
supporting_quotes: People may want a calm environment, but they don't want a monotonous or boring environment, they might want an exciting environment, they don't want a chaotic environment. Acoustic boredom, being in a monotonous acoustic environment is just as frustrating as being in a chaotic environment because they are both unwanted. It is not a function of the decibel level, it's a function of the perceptual response in context

findings.antecedent: Occupant control over the environment (e.g., opening windows)
findings.consequent: Moderated cognitive response, reduced stress, increased satisfaction, but potential for adverse health effects if wrongly targeted
findings.description: Control opportunities can positively influence perception and reduce stress, similar to adaptive thermal comfort. However, poorly targeted control (e.g., opening windows for thermal comfort leading to noise exposure) can create new health risks.
supporting_quotes: From a pure soundscape perspective we would say, if I am choosing, I have control over my environment, I know if I am going to open this window I am going to hear some unwanted sounds but I may prefer that than this monotonous environment that is driving me crazy ... you may then not have the stress response that you have when you feel angry about the noise and no control to stop it

The key thing is about occupant control of the environment because when the occupants have control over their environment, they feel differently about it so they may rate it differently ... That concept of having control over the environment changing your response to certain environmental conditions is embedded in the adaptive thermal comfort model

findings.antecedent: Holistic and integrated design (resolving trade-offs at design stage)
findings.consequent: Maximized benefits from building performance, reduced burden on occupants to choose between comforts, reduced health risks
findings.description: Ideal design resolves trade-offs between different comfort domains (e.g., thermal, acoustic) at the design stage, preventing occupants from having to make choices that could lead to health risks, and maximizing benefits from building energy performance capabilities.
supporting_quotes: It is not ideal. Ideal would be that people would not have to make a choice between thermal and acoustic comfort and noise pollution

derived_hypotheses: Perceptual dimensions underlying the affective response to the indoor acoustic environment can be identified, accounting for indoor peculiarities and varying expectations/needs.
Indoor soundscape descriptors can be used to define a reference system for measurement, allowing visualization in a perceptual space and setting design targets.
Multi-domain approaches will better capture human-building interactions and the multifactorial nature of human experience in soundscape models.
Existing outdoor soundscape data collection methods can be tailored and applied to indoor environments, including soundwalks, mobile apps, and non-participatory observations.
Soundscape methodologies can be integrated into POE practices and building certification protocols to collect evidence of positive impacts and successes, not just failures.
New scientific evidence will inform the relationship between tasks, cognitive/emotional states, and wanted sounds, moving from pathogenic to salutogenic models.
New noise exposure thresholds can be identified, varying with space use, control, and exposure time, below which soundscape methodologies are applied.
Strategies allowing building occupants to adapt and tailor their personal acoustic environment will yield benefits, ranging from manual window opening to advanced IoT-based systems.
Scientific evidence is needed to 'measure' the benefits of natural sounds and guide their reproduction indoors for biophilic purposes, and to exploit urban sounds for sense of place.
Soundscape strategies should be implemented first at an urban scale, then at a building scale, through integrated urban design and planning.
Indoor soundscape indices and new prediction models can be developed by triangulating physical and perceptual data.
Virtual reality technologies can be improved for ecological validity and accessibility to practitioners for pre-construction soundscape assessments.
mechanism_candidates: Human perceptual response to acoustic stimuli in context
Multisensory interaction of the acoustic sense with all other senses
Sound as a design 'resource' for shaping healthy and supportive acoustic environments
Perceptual modulation by context and expectations
Reverberant sound field amplifying sound disturbance
Masking unwanted sounds by desired sounds (indoor/outdoor)
Personal control over acoustic environment moderating cognitive response and stress
Coherent combination of visual and audio stimuli enhancing environmental appreciation and physiological stress recovery
Shift from pathogenic (absence of disease) to salutogenic (health promotion) model of building design
Exploiting hedonic potential of sounds to support optimal task performance and generate positive health/well-being
transferability_limits: Findings are based on a restricted number of experts with specific backgrounds (acoustic research, public health, well-being, building design, urban planning).
The exploratory nature of the study means findings provide initial expert opinions for preliminary discussion, not comprehensive coverage of all viewpoints.
Further quantitative and/or qualitative oriented research projects are needed to analyze and review the generated hypotheses.
limitations: The study was limited by the selection of a restricted number of experts with a background in acoustic research, public health and well-being, building design and urban planning.

Interviewees were not chosen to comprehensively cover the many possible viewpoints that can be found in the scientific community but to provide initial expert opinions for establishing a preliminary discussion in the field of indoor soundscape research.
This approach is in line with the purpose of using expert interviews as an exploratory tool.

Exploratory interviews helped to structure the subject under investigation, to highlight knowledge gaps and to generate hypotheses to be further analyzed and reviewed in future quantitative and/or qualitative oriented research projects.

paper_metadata.title: Acoustics for Supportive and Healthy Buildings: Emerging Themes on Indoor Soundscape Research
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Acoustics for Supportive and Healthy Buildings: Emerging Themes on Indoor Soundscape Research
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The focus of the building industry and research is shifting from delivering satisfactory spaces to going beyond what is merely acceptable with a wave of new research and practice dedicated to exploring how the built environment can support task performance and enhance people’s health and well-being. The present study addresses the role of acoustics in this paradigm shift. Indoor soundscape research has recently emerged as an approach that brings a perceptual perspective on building and room acoustics in order to shape built environments that “sound good” according to building occupants’ preference and needs. This paper establishes an initial discussion over some of the open questions in this field of research that is still in an embryonic stage. A thematic analysis of structured interviews with a panel of experts offered a range of perspectives on the characterization, management, and design of indoor soundscapes and health-related outcomes. The discussion pointed out the importance of both perceptual and multisensory research and integrated participatory design practices to enable a holistic view regarding the complex building–user interrelations and the design of just cities. Soundscape methodologies tailored to the peculiarities of indoor soundscapes can help to measure and predict the human perceptual response to the acoustic stimuli in context, thus reducing the risk of mismatches between expected and real building experiences. This perceptual perspective is expected to widen the scientific evidence for the negative and positive impacts of the acoustic environment on human health, well-being, and quality of life. This will support prioritizing the role of acoustics in building design and challenge many current design practices that are based on a noise control approach.

instruments_used.name: Interview Protocol
instruments_used.construct: Perceptions of indoor soundscapes, acoustic quality, and their impact on health and well-being in buildings
instruments_used.description: A set of open-ended questions used to gather qualitative data from participants regarding their experiences and opinions on acoustic environments in buildings and current building design processes.
